LGBTQIA is an acronym — a word formed from the first letters of other words. Each letter represents a group of people who share a similar experience of either their gender identity (how they feel about their own gender on the inside) or their sexual/romantic orientation (who they are attracted to). You will often see a plus sign added at the end, making it LGBTQIA+, to acknowledge that there are even more identities beyond what the letters individually cover.

Before diving into each letter, it is important to understand two foundational ideas that will make everything else click.
Two Foundational Ideas You Must Understand First

1. Sexual Orientation

Sexual orientation refers to who a person is emotionally, romantically, or sexually attracted to. A man who is exclusively attracted to women, for example, has a heterosexual (straight) orientation. But attraction does not always follow this pattern — some people are attracted to the same gender, to multiple genders, or to no one at all. Several letters in LGBTQIA describe different sexual orientations.

2. Gender Identity

Gender identity is a person's deep, internal sense of their own gender — whether they feel like a man, a woman, both, neither, or something else entirely. This is separate from the sex a person is assigned at birth (based on their physical body), and it is also separate from sexual orientation. Your gender identity is about who you are, not who you are attracted to.

Keeping these two ideas distinct is crucial, because some letters in LGBTQIA relate to sexual orientation, while others relate to gender identity — and confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes people make.

L — Lesbian

A lesbian is a woman who is romantically and/or sexually attracted to other women. The word comes from the name of the Greek island of Lesbos, where the ancient poet Sappho wrote about love between women. Today, some people whose gender falls outside the strict male/female divide also identify with the term lesbian if it feels right to them.

G — Gay

Gay most commonly refers to a man who is romantically and/or sexually attracted to other men. However, the word is also used more broadly as an umbrella term for the entire LGBTQIA community (as in "gay rights" or "the gay community"). Some women also prefer to identify as gay rather than lesbian — both are valid. The word originally just meant "happy" in English, but it gradually shifted in meaning over the 20th century to refer to same-sex attraction.

B — Bisexual

Bisexual (often shortened to "bi") describes a person who is romantically and/or sexually attracted to more than one gender — for example, to people of their own gender and to people of other genders as well. A widespread misconception is that bisexuality only means attraction to men and women, but most definitions include attraction to non-binary people too. Bisexuality does not mean a person is confused, "going through a phase," or equally attracted to all genders — the degree of attraction can vary from person to person, and even shift over time.

T — Transgender

Transgender (often shortened to "trans") relates to gender identity, not sexual orientation. A transgender person is someone whose gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth. For example, someone assigned male at birth who identifies as a woman is a transgender woman. Someone assigned female at birth who identifies as a man is a transgender man.

Some transgender people choose to transition — a process that can involve changing their name, pronouns, clothing style, or even undergoing hormone therapy or surgery — but not all do, and a person is no less transgender if they do not transition. Being transgender says nothing about who a person is attracted to. A transgender person can be straight, gay, bisexual, or any other orientation.

A useful contrasting word here is cisgender (often shortened to "cis") — this describes a person whose gender identity does match the sex they were assigned at birth. It is simply the opposite of transgender, and is not a negative word.

Q — Queer (and sometimes Questioning)

The letter Q most commonly stands for Queer. Historically, "queer" was used as a hurtful slur against LGBTQIA people. However, beginning in the late 20th century, many within the community reclaimed the word and now use it with pride. Today, "queer" serves as a broad, flexible umbrella term for anyone who is not heterosexual and/or not cisgender. People who feel that specific labels like "gay" or "bisexual" do not quite capture their experience often prefer to simply call themselves queer.

Because of its history as a slur, not everyone in the community is comfortable with the word. It is generally best practice to use it only when describing someone who uses it to describe themselves — never apply it to someone as a label they did not choose.

The Q can also stand for Questioning — referring to people who are actively exploring or figuring out their sexual orientation or gender identity and have not yet settled on a label. This acknowledges that understanding yourself is sometimes a journey, not a single moment.

I — Intersex

Intersex refers to people who are born with natural variations in their biological sex characteristics — such as their chromosomes, hormones, genitalia, or reproductive anatomy — that do not fit neatly into the typical medical definitions of "male" or "female." For example, a person might be born with both XX and XY chromosomes, or with hormone levels that differ from what is considered typical for either sex.

Intersex is a biological characteristic, not a gender identity or a sexual orientation. Intersex people can be straight, gay, bisexual, transgender, or anything else — being intersex does not determine who they are attracted to or how they identify. Intersex variations are more common than most people realize, and researchers estimate that roughly 1.7% of people are born with some form of intersex trait, though estimates vary depending on the definition used.

Historically, many intersex infants were subjected to non-consensual surgical procedures to make their bodies conform to binary male or female norms. A central goal of intersex advocacy is ending such medically unnecessary surgeries performed without the individual's informed consent.

A — Asexual (and Aromantic, and sometimes Ally)

The A most widely and accurately stands for Asexual (often shortened to "ace"). An asexual person experiences little to no sexual attraction to anyone, regardless of gender. This is a sexual orientation, just like being gay or straight — it is not a choice, not a medical problem, and not the same as simply deciding to abstain from sex. Asexual people can still experience deep romantic feelings, form meaningful relationships, and live fulfilling lives.

Closely related is Aromantic (often shortened to "aro") — a person who experiences little to no romantic attraction to others. It is important to understand the difference: sexual attraction is about wanting a sexual connection with someone, while romantic attraction is about wanting a romantic, loving relationship. These can exist independently. Some people are both asexual and aromantic (called "aroace"), while others may be one but not the other. The aromantic identity is often grouped under the A as well, since it falls within the same broader spectrum.

The A is sometimes said to stand for Ally — a person who is not LGBTQIA themselves but actively supports and stands up for the community. However, many LGBTQIA people prefer not to include allies under the acronym, since the letters primarily represent identities rather than a stance of support.

When you see LGBTQIA+, the plus sign is a catch-all symbol acknowledging that there are many more identities and experiences that the letters do not individually name. Here are some of the most common ones included under the "+":

Pansexual — A pansexual person is attracted to people regardless of their gender. The prefix "pan" means "all." While this sounds similar to bisexual, many pansexual people describe the distinction as this: their attraction is entirely gender-blind — a person's gender simply does not factor into who they are drawn to.

Nonbinary — A nonbinary person does not identify exclusively as a man or as a woman. Their gender identity falls outside the traditional male-female binary. Nonbinary is itself a broad umbrella term that includes more specific identities, such as:

  • Genderfluid — a person whose gender identity shifts or moves over time.
  • Agender — a person who feels they have no gender, or whose gender is essentially neutral or absent.
  • Genderqueer — a person whose gender falls outside conventional categories.

Demisexual — A person who only experiences sexual attraction after forming a deep emotional bond with someone. Demisexuality is considered part of the asexual spectrum.

Two-Spirit — A term used by some Indigenous peoples of North America to describe a person who fulfills a traditional role that incorporates both masculine and feminine qualities. It carries deep cultural and spiritual significance and is specific to Indigenous cultures — it should not be used by or applied to non-Indigenous people.

The "+" ensures that no one's identity is rendered invisible simply because the acronym runs out of letters.

The acronym exists because LGBTQIA people have historically faced — and in many parts of the world continue to face — discrimination, violence, unequal legal treatment, and social rejection, simply for being who they are. Uniting under a shared label helps these groups build community, advocate collectively for equal rights and dignity, and signal solidarity with one another. While each letter represents a distinct experience, they are connected by a common history of marginalization and a shared pursuit of respect and equality.
How the Acronym Has Evolved Over Time

The acronym did not always look the way it does today. For much of the 20th century, the movement centered on "gay and lesbian" identities. By the late 1980s and 1990s, bisexual and transgender people pushed for recognition and inclusion, giving rise to "LGBT." As visibility grew for more identities, additional letters were incorporated — first "LGBTQ," then "LGBTQIA," and now commonly "LGBTQIA+." This evolution reflects a broader shift in society's understanding of gender and sexuality — from a rigid binary view toward a more nuanced, inclusive picture of human experience.
Key Distinctions to Always Keep in Mind

Sexual orientation and gender identity are different things. Who you are attracted to is separate from who you feel you are. A transgender woman, for example, could be attracted to men, women, both, or no one — her gender identity does not determine her orientation.

Sex assigned at birth, gender identity, and gender expression are three different things. Your biological sex (assigned at birth based on physical characteristics) differs from your gender identity (how you feel on the inside) and your gender expression (how you present yourself to the world through clothing, mannerisms, and so on). These three can align in different ways for different people.

Being LGBTQIA is not a choice. The broad consensus of the global medical and scientific community — including the World Health Organization and the American Psychological Association — is that sexual orientation and gender identity are not chosen. Attempts to change a person's orientation or identity through so-called "conversion therapy" are considered harmful and ineffective.

"Queer" is both an identity and an umbrella term, but use it carefully. Only use it about people who use it to describe themselves.

LGBTQIA people are not a monolith. Under this single acronym are people of every race, culture, religion, nationality, age, and background. They hold vastly varied views, experiences, and ways of living. The acronym represents a community, not a uniform group.

To bring it all together: LGBTQIA stands for Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer (or Questioning), Intersex, and Asexual (and Aromantic). The "+" includes many additional identities like pansexual, nonbinary, demisexual, and more. Some letters (L, G, B, Q, A) relate to sexual or romantic orientation — who a person is attracted to. Others (T, and partly Q and nonbinary under the +) relate to gender identity — who a person is. Intersex (I) is unique in referring to biological characteristics present at birth. The acronym as a whole represents people whose identities fall outside what has historically been considered the default — heterosexual and cisgender — and who have come together to advocate for recognition, rights, and dignity.
